source: Maglio & Wenger (2000) Two views are better than one: epistemic actions may prime
finding: Opened the full PDF this session (via WebFetch binary save, then pdftotext). Gap 4 check: the odd statistics are printed in the original, so b07 quoted them faithfully. A single preview of a falling piece raised accuracy and cut reaction time in a memory-priming task.
numbers: N=30 psychology students, 3 days x 480 trials, 3x3x3x3x2x3x2 mixed design. One preview vs none: accuracy .86 vs .53, t(1,59)=33.85, p<.001; RT 869 vs 1791 ms, t(1,59)=2.01, p<.05. Direct vs indirect memory test accuracy .95 vs .88, F(1,25)=4.59. Number of previews (1 vs 2), retention interval and zoid type: all F<1 on accuracy.
quote: two different views of a falling zoid are better than one
limits: df=59 does not fit N=30 and the F tests use df=25, so degrees of freedom are inconsistent in the original (likely pooling that is not explained). A t of 33.85 is an artefact of that. A 922 ms RT gap with t=2.01 is also odd. Direction is plausible, size and tests are unreliable. The preview is supplied by the experimenter, not made by the player.
agent_relevance: Weak human anchor: a cheap extra view helps by priming memory, not by replacing mental rotation. Do not cite the t values.

source: Maglio, Wenger & Copeland (2003) The benefits of epistemic action outweigh the costs
finding: Opened the full PDF this session. Same lab, new sample, cleaner statistics. Previews sped responses, raised processing capacity by about 38 percent, and the benefit exceeded the estimated cost of the extra actions at every lag.
numbers: N=15 students, single session. Mean RT 528 ms (preview) vs 673 ms (no preview), t=5.09, p<.0001. Hazard-function regression: preview presence +37.8 percent capacity; lag x presence +33.6; orientation x presence +11.5. Benefit/cost ratio reliably above 1 at lags 0, 1, 2 and rising with lag, F(2,28)=31.25. Cost = 2x mean keypress RT added to a fixed 4.4 s trial time.
quote: the benefits more than outweighed the costs in all cases
limits: The authors say the results replicate their 2000 and 2002 work, so this is a same-lab replication, not independent. Cost is a keypress proxy, not real rotations. Previews were shown by the experimenter. N=15.
agent_relevance: Best human evidence that the benefit of a cheap information-revealing step can be priced against its cost. Supports a value-of-information rule for probing (gap 2) in principle.

source: Gap 4 note: independent replication of Maglio & Wenger 2000 / Maglio et al 2003
finding: No independent-lab replication found. The only follow-ups I could open are by the same authors (the 2003 paper says it replicates 2000 and 2002). Search APIs were rate-limited or out of quota, so absence is not proven.
numbers: 0 independent replications found; 2 same-lab papers opened (d01, d02).
limits: WebSearch quota gone; arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned 429 during this pass.
agent_relevance: Keep K04 as single-source. Do not treat the priming result as a replicated finding.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: Opened the paper. Gap 1 and 5: with the same candidate patches, majority vote alone solves 77 of 300 SWE-bench Lite issues. Adding model-written reproduction tests (a step that runs code) lifts it to 96 (32.0 percent) for about 0.25 dollars extra per issue. The tests filter patches.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite N=300, GPT-4o. Majority vote only 77 (25.67%, $0.00); +regression tests 81 (27.0%, $0.01); +reproduction tests 96 (32.0%, $0.25). Total cost $0.70 per issue. Gains from more samples plateau at about 40 samples. Upper bound with a perfect pick is 126 (42.0%). Open agent systems cost more in the same table (SWE-agent GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62).
limits: Reproduction tests are generated by the same model and used to filter, not to guide, the attempt. Not a toy-input probe before a first attempt. Single model family, mid-2024.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'a test run beats extra votes at similar cost': the executing step adds information that more votes do not.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Opened the paper. Resampling is a strong baseline when an automatic verifier exists, and weak when it does not. Without an executable check, majority voting and reward models plateau after several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art then 43%). Coverage grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. Voting and reward-model selection plateau beyond several hundred samples.
quote: coverage scales with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude
limits: Coverage means 'any sample correct' and needs a verifier to realise. Earlier models. No probe-first arm.
agent_relevance: The fair rival to probe-first is verifier-backed resampling. Our test must match tokens against it, and the verifier is itself a probe.

source: Zhong, Wang & Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB, a large language model debugger via verifying runtime execution step by step
finding: Opened the paper. Runtime values from actually running code beat the model's own dry-run or explanation. The gain is large for a weaker seed program and small for a stronger one. Gap 3 (strength) and gap 5 (probe kind).
numbers: HumanEval, debugger GPT-3.5. Seed GPT-3.5 73.8: Self-Debugging +7.3, LDB +9.1 (82.9). Seed GPT-4 87.2: SD +1.2, LDB +2.4 (89.6). Seed Reflexion 91.5: SD +0.6, LDB +3.6 (95.1). Gains up to 9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. Repeated sampling and Self-Debugging (explain/trace) stall after about 2-3 rounds; LDB keeps rising.
quote: actual runtime execution information significantly helps LLMs
limits: Debugger is GPT-3.5 in these rows, so seed strength and debugger strength are mixed. Pass@1 on small benchmarks near ceiling.
agent_relevance: Gains from the execution probe shrink as the seed gets stronger but do not vanish. Self-trace without a real run is the weak arm.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: large language models can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Opened the paper. Same loop with and without the external tool: the tool is the active ingredient. The model's own critique adds about nothing and can hurt. Gap 5 and gap 8.
numbers: HotpotQA F1 (text-davinci-003 / ChatGPT): CoT 46.1 / 42.8; CRITIC 50.5 / 52.9; CRITIC w/o Tool 46.1 / 46.1. Own critique alone: -0.03 and +2.33 F1 averaged over datasets for the two models. Math program synthesis, davinci-003 GSM8K: PoT 70.1, CRITIC 72.2 (+2.1), CRITIC w/o Tool 68.3 (-1.8). The paper says CRITIC works better with more powerful LLMs.
quote: Tool-interaction plays a critical role in CRITIC
limits: Tool is search or interpreter, not toy-input probing. 2023-era models. Some table columns are garbled in the PDF text, so cells were cross-read against the summary text.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a real signal beats the model grading itself. It also says stronger models get more from the tool, which cuts against d06.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Opened the paper. With no oracle label, asking the model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. Oracle-label gains in earlier papers come from knowing when to stop. Gap 8: self-generated feedback can harm.
numbers: GPT-3.5 over two rounds: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 59.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and flips correct to wrong more often than wrong to right.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Reflection with no external signal, not probing. 2023 models. 200 questions per set for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: A probe that returns no independent signal, or a toy case the model judges itself, is just more reflection. Anchoring risk is real when the model interprets its own output.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction of LLMs
finding: Opened the abstract and introduction. The survey says no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted model alone, except on tasks suited to it. It works where reliable external feedback exists, and the bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Three headline findings: (1) no demonstration of self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback outside suited tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback (code interpreter, search); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
quote: the bottleneck is in the feedback generation
limits: Survey, not new measurements. Read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Probes should return signal from outside the model (execution, tests, lookups). Judge-yourself probes should not be trusted.

source: Mundler et al. (2025) SWT-Bench: testing and validating real-world bug-fixes with code agents
finding: Opened the paper. Agents can write issue-reproducing tests, and telling the agent to run its tests before submitting raised success. Generated tests double the precision of proposed fixes.
numbers: SWE-agent test success rate S 15.9% -> 18.5% when told to execute tests before submitting (SWE-agent+). Tests generated for up to 87% of issues. Keeping only fixes where all generated tests are fail-to-pass or pass-to-pass doubled SWE-agent precision to 47.8% at about 20% recall.
quote: tests are an effective filter for proposed code fixes
limits: Precision rises because recall drops to 20%. A filter, not a pre-attempt probe. GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: An execute-your-probe step gives a real gain at small cost, but it trades coverage for precision.

source: Yang et al. (2023) InterCode: standardizing and benchmarking interactive coding with execution feedback
finding: Opened the paper. Letting models see execution feedback over up to 10 turns multiplies success, most for the strongest model on SQL. But the Try Again loop stops when reward=1, which uses an oracle.
numbers: InterCode-SQL single turn vs Try Again (n=10): GPT-4 9.1 -> 73.7, GPT-3.5 10.5 -> 47.3, text-davinci-003 7.4 -> 15.6, StarChat-16B 8.9 -> 9.7, Vicuna-13B 2.6 -> 6.3. Bash: GPT-4 34.0 -> 48.5, GPT-3.5 34.5 -> 46.5. ReAct on GPT-3.5 SQL 47.3 -> 58.7.
quote: performance is superior in the interactive setting for all models
limits: Try Again terminates on the true reward, so gains are an upper bound. Weak models (Vicuna, StarChat) gain almost nothing. Single turn is zero-shot with no schema, which inflates the gap.
agent_relevance: Cuts against 'gains shrink with strength': here gains rise with strength because weak models cannot use feedback. A hump shape is plausible.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: program-aided language models
finding: Opened the paper. Offloading arithmetic to a program (an executed step) helps modestly on GSM8K and hugely when the numbers get hard. Closest LLM analog to Kirsh's coin counting with hands.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT Minerva 540B 65.6 vs PAL Codex 72.0. GSM-HARD (large numbers): CoT 65.6 -> 20.1 (about 70% relative drop), PAL stays about 61. Majority voting lifts PAL 72.0 -> 80.4.
limits: CoT and PAL use different models in the headline row (Minerva vs Codex). Offloading, not information probing. Text says 61.5 for PAL on GSM-HARD, table shows 61.2.
agent_relevance: Execution beats in-head reasoning when the step is mechanical. Fits K05.

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: self-aware agent for tool overuse mitigation
finding: Opened the paper. Agents call tools when they do not need to, and sometimes the tool call makes the answer wrong. A trained agent that decides when to use tools cut calls and raised accuracy. Gap 2.
numbers: Base models invoke tools unnecessarily over 30% of the time (Llama over 50%). SMARTAgent: tool use -24.0% (macro average), performance +37.1% (macro average). 7B matches the 70B counterpart and GPT-4o. On out-of-distribution GSM8K and MINTQA it keeps accuracy with one-fifth the tool calls.
limits: Trained on supervised data about when tools are needed, so not a prompt-only rule. Baselines are other tool-using policies.
agent_relevance: Always-probe is not free. A learned gate on when to probe is the tested alternative, and it helped.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Opened the paper. The best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty for that model. Allocating adaptively beats best-of-N by over 4x efficiency. Closest quantitative value-of-computation rule to gap 2.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy: more than 4x efficiency over best-of-N. Where the small model has non-trivial success, test-time compute beats a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched test. On hard questions pretraining is preferable once inference load is high. Difficulty binned into five levels from 2048 samples per problem (oracle), or model-predicted.
quote: effectiveness of different approaches critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt
limits: Math (MATH) with PaLM 2-S and verifiers, not probing. The difficulty estimate costs compute itself.
agent_relevance: Supports gating: choose probe, think, or resample per item by estimated difficulty.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking progress in automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Opened the paper. LLM agents choose experiments in 10 probabilistic worlds and are scored by expected information gain. All tested systems struggle at choosing informative experiments. Gap 6.
numbers: 10 environments, error bars over 5 runs. Models: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, Qwen2.5 7B/32B, OpenThinker 7B/32B. 32B beat 7B. Instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 beat reasoning-tuned OpenThinker. GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret. Box's Apprentice (fits explicit models) did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o. Strong on population growth and death process, weak on hyperbolic discounting.
quote: all current approaches struggle with both experimental design and model discovery
limits: Exact numeric tables are in figures. No 2026 frontier models. No arm that enumerates and scores candidate probes with an external scorer.
agent_relevance: Choosing the probe is a separate skill and weak. Reasoning-tuned models did not win here.

source: Feng et al. (2025) ReTool: reinforcement learning for strategic tool use in LLMs
finding: Opened the abstract, Figure 1 and the response-length section. Letting a long-reasoning model run code mid-thought, with RL on when to call it, beat text-only RL on hard math with fewer training steps. Gap 1 and 3.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: AIME 2024 67.0% (400 steps) vs text RL 40.0% (1080 steps); AIME 2025 49.3 vs 36.7; extended setting 72.5%. Response length falls about 40% after RL (10k to 6k tokens); code calls move earlier in the response.
limits: Training comparison, not a prompting test. Not token-matched at inference. The model is trained to use the tool, so it is not evidence for scaffold-only gains.
agent_relevance: Execution beats pure text reasoning on hard math for a reasoning model and uses fewer tokens, so the token-matched case looks favourable.

source: Gap note: name search for epistemic action, complementary action or interactive perception in LLM papers
finding: Gap 7 stays open. WebSearch quota was used up; arXiv API, arXiv search, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all returned HTTP 429 in this pass. I opened adjacent papers by known id (d04-d16) and none frames its probe as an epistemic action in Kirsh and Maglio's sense.
numbers: 0 named-term LLM papers found; 13 adjacent LLM papers opened.
limits: Absence is not shown, only that the search was blocked.
agent_relevance: Treat the direct test as ours to run. The adjacent literature is enough to design it.

source: Destefano, Lindstedt & Gray (2011) Use of complementary actions decreases with expertise (CogSci 33)
finding: Gap 6. The only large-sample test of the skill claim. 59 Tetris players across a very wide skill range. Complementary actions were defined by five rules applied to game logs. Rates fell with skill. The most lenient rules show a hump: a rise at low skill, then a fall. Stricter rules show almost none at any level.
numbers: 59 players, 173 games, two tournaments. Qualifying top scores 867 to 236,305; best single game 1,023,941; 25 of 173 games above 100,000. No player above 100,000 points used medium or strict translation actions in more than 2% of episodes. The 1.02M-point game had a 0.08 lenient translation rate, 1 over-rotation and 5 both-direction rotations in 1,281 episodes. Authors infer Maglio and Kirsh's two 20-hour players were at the level of their lowest two score bins (about 10,000 points or less).
quote: complementary actions decrease with expertise, regardless of the criterion used
limits: Classification is by algorithm on logs, not by intent; goal switching and slips are confounded with lenient rules (authors say so). The match of the old players to score bins is an inference. Tournament entrants, not a trained sample. Conference paper, no inferential statistics reported. Early rotations that reveal a half-visible piece are not counted as complementary here, unlike in Kirsh and Maglio.
agent_relevance: Probe rate should not be assumed to rise with familiarity. A hump (probe while learning a task type, less once the answer pattern is known) fits the agent: probe early on an unfamiliar task type, cut probes when the pattern is known. Do not cite 'epistemic action increases with skill' as a design rule.

source: Kumar, Kumar, Ahuja & Jha (2026) Towards a belief-based world model for LLM agents
finding: Gap 8. A 2026 paper that uses the named distinction (cites Kirsh and Maglio 1994) and runs experiments. It gives the policy a query action that reveals what is known and unknown about the hidden state (where could the object be). That belief query raised reward within a step budget in the text worlds tested. It added to a simulation tool (WALL-E) rather than replacing it. A memory-only ablation did less than the belief.
numbers: ALFWorld, ScienceWorld (24 task types), BabyAI-Text (4 BALROG tasks). Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B with ReAct and ReflAct, plus Claude Sonnet; three runs (not for Sonnet). Metric: reward vs fraction of step budget. Exact values are in figures only, so no numbers could be read. Text claims: the combined model beat the base agent in all cases; Sonnet nearly saturates ALFWorld and ScienceWorld (small efficiency gains) but gains were substantial on BabyAI where it is not saturated. A Zipf (1.25) prior test checks whether probabilities matter beyond the candidate set.
quote: epistemic actions are information-gathering actions that primarily reduce uncertainty about the current state
limits: The belief is hand-built per benchmark, not learned. The query is answered by an environment-side model, so this tests information access, not the agent's choice of when to probe. Figures only. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that an explicit 'what do I not know yet' query helps weaker models and hard tasks and adds little for a strong model on easy tasks. Candidate for S4: list the unknown state and query it before acting. Test it as an arm.

source: Qian et al. (2026) Current agents fail to leverage world model as tool for foresight (ACL 2026)
finding: Gap 3. Giving agents a simulator tool does not by itself help. Some agents almost never call it, some misread its output, and forcing calls can hurt. The main bottleneck is when to call, how to read the result, and how to use it afterwards.
numbers: Nine vision-language models. Agent tasks use a ground-truth simulator; VQA tasks use Wan2.1 video generation. Some agents invoke simulation in under 1% of cases; about 15% of used rollouts are misused; performance is inconsistent and falls by up to 5% when simulation is available or enforced. Manual analysis of 60 cases; automated labels agree with humans in 81.67% of them. Invocation does not simply rise with model scale; Llama variants are more willing, GPT and Qwen variants often decline.
limits: Foresight tool is a simulator, not a code probe; vision-language models; the video simulator is imperfect in VQA. Percentages are the paper's summary figures; per-model tables are large and were not all checked.
agent_relevance: A probe tool alone is not a policy. The schema needs an explicit rule for when to call (low confidence, hidden state) and a step that says what the result changed. Matches SMART (d13).

source: Ceka et al. (2026) Understanding automated program repair agents through the lens of traceability (ISSTA)
finding: Gaps 2, 4, 10. Trace study of 5 repair agents on 500 tasks. Agents whose workflow forces a reproduction step write reproducers on almost all tasks. But a reproducer triggers the bug only about half the time, and patches that pass the agent's own reproducer often fail the real tests. Success falls steeply with difficulty.
numbers: 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 5 agents, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and GPT-4o. Success 66-73% on easy vs 4.8-19% on hard, none on very hard. Workflow agents (Agentless, ACR, MASAI) write reproducers for all tasks; open-process agents under 80% (except OpenHands with Claude). Reproducers trigger the bug in 41-57%. Overfitting (pass own reproducer, fail real tests): SWE-agent 17-26% (18-30% in the reproducer analysis), Agentless 4-5%. Bug-localization context raised successful reproductions from 614 to 697 of 1,500 samples (13.5% relative) and helped 54% of issues (27 of 50). Higher temperature gave more distinct errors (2.08 to 2.76) but lower success.
limits: Observational trace analysis; reproduce-first is not randomised, so it cannot show that probing causes better fixes. 2024-era models. Agentless trajectories came from a third-party release.
agent_relevance: A self-written probe can be wrong or too weak. Rule: the probe must fail on the broken case before it is trusted, and a pass on your own test is not proof. This is the misleading-probe risk (gap 10), measured at 17-30% for open-process agents.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Agentic bug reproduction for effective automated program repair at Google
finding: Gap 2. A generated reproduction test, given to a repair agent as an input before it starts, helped it fix more bugs and in fewer steps. This is steering, not only selection. The same tests also rank candidate fixes.
numbers: 80 human-reported Google bugs. BRT Agent made plausible reproduction tests for 28% vs 10% for LIBRO. On the 23 bugs with a plausible test: the repair agent (Passerine, Gemini, 20 runs per bug, temperature 0.2) got a plausible fix on 17 of 23 (74%) with the test vs 13 of 23 (57%) without; 6 bugs were solved only with it. Chance of a plausible fix given the test was used 33% vs 2% when not used. Fewer steps with the test (max 25). Selection by the Ensemble Pass Rate chose a plausible fix from 20 candidates in 70% of cases at top-1.
limits: Small: 23 bugs. 'Plausible' tests were defined by failing before and passing after the true fix, so the test given to the repair agent was oracle-filtered; a real pipeline would not know which test is good. Proprietary code and a fine-tuned editing model. 11% of plausible patches changed existing tests.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that a probe result passed forward to the next attempt (not just used to rerank) changes outcomes. The effect is probably an upper bound because the test was oracle-filtered. Supports an S4 test: probe output fed to attempt 2 vs probe used only to choose among attempts.

source: Shen et al. (2025) Thinking vs. doing: agents that reason by scaling test-time interaction
finding: Gap 1. For a web agent, spending budget on more interaction steps beat spending it on longer thinking per step, in a prompted setting with a small model. Prompted re-checking helped on average but sometimes flipped correct answers.
numbers: Gemma 3 12B prompted agent, WebArena subset, 3 runs. Action-only 14.76% task success; chain of thought 23.81%. Strategies (task success %): check-again 26.14; budget forcing 24.81; best-of-n 25.03; check-again + budget forcing 26.33; check-again + best-of-n 27.36. After a double-check the agent changed its action 25% of the time; under budget forcing only 15%, mostly reordering sub-tasks. The trained TTI model improved over its base by about 9% and 8% on two web benchmarks.
limits: 'Check again' is more interaction, not a probe of a hidden fact. Gains of 1 to 3 points are small for 3 runs. One small model. Authors note repeated re-checking can turn right answers wrong (the Map domain dropped).
agent_relevance: Weak support for probe over think at equal budget, and a warning: prompt-only extra passes can regress. Run U1 with a real executable probe, not a re-check prompt.

source: Lindenbauer et al. (2025) The complexity trap: simple observation masking is as efficient as LLM summarization for agent context management
finding: Gap 9. Probe output piles up in the history. Hiding old tool outputs (keep the last 10 turns) cut cost by more than half and did not lower the solve rate. Summarising with a model did no better. In three of five setups the cheapest strategy also solved more than keeping everything.
numbers: SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified (500 instances), five model setups. Observation masking window M=10. Qwen3-Coder 480B: masking 52% cheaper than the raw agent and +2.6 points solve rate; also $0.03 per instance ($15 over 500) cheaper than LLM-Summary. Both strategies cut cost per instance by over 50% in most setups. A hybrid cuts a further 7% (vs masking) and 11% (vs summary). LLM-Summary lengthened trajectories ('trajectory elongation') because it hides failure signals.
limits: One scaffold (plus an initial OpenHands check). Software tasks only. The reasoning model Qwen3-32B (thinking) was an outlier.
agent_relevance: Probe outputs should be short and old ones dropped. Keep the conclusion of each probe, not its raw output. Summaries that hide failures can make the agent run longer.

source: Sun, Min, Chang & Bisk (2024) Tools fail: detecting silent errors in faulty tools
finding: Gap 10. When a tool silently returns a wrong answer, models copy it. A one-line warning that tools can be wrong helps a lot. Detection of tool errors is only moderate.
numbers: Calculator task with perturbed outputs; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Command-R, Command-R+, Gemini-1.5. With a broken calculator accuracy fell up to 47% below the best no-tool setting; models copy the wrong output with a made-up justification. A disclaimer raised accuracy by up to 30%; chain of thought and examples brought it near the best no-tool score. In ALFRED (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro) accept/reject detection reached F1 60-70 with interventions. Chain of thought sometimes did worse by wrongly rejecting correct output.
limits: 2024 models; synthetic perturbations; a calculator is a narrow domain. No test with 2026 frontier models.
agent_relevance: A probe result is a claim, not a fact. Add a line to S4: the output may be wrong; compare it with what you expected before using it. Test it (U7).

source: Annese et al. (2025) Who sees what? Structured thought-action sequences for epistemic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Gaps 3, 8. Small study of a ReAct agent (o3-mini) that may take ASK actions in a perspective-taking household task. Planner-derived examples of optimal epistemic action did not give steady gains. The agent asked more than the planner optimum and failed where it had to reason about hidden space.
numbers: Seven scenario types, five trials each, o3-mini Director and Matcher. First-take accuracy was 100% in Perspective, Hidden, Base and Near and 0-40% in Far, Not-That and Distractor across example types; the no-example baseline was similar. Average steps 2.97-3.26 with examples vs 3.11 without vs 2.14 for the planner. Average ASK actions 0.83-1.06 with examples vs 0.91 without vs 0.43 for the planner.
limits: Tiny design (5 trials, one model). The table layout in the PDF text is partly garbled, so the mapping of numbers to scenarios was read with care. Not a code probe.
agent_relevance: Agents over-ask relative to a planner and do not improve from examples. A cost term on probing needs explicit modelling, not only demonstrations.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable code actions elicit better LLM agents (CodeAct)
finding: Gaps 4, 7. Letting the model act by writing code that runs (and reads back errors) beat JSON or text actions on success and used fewer turns. The advantage got larger for stronger models.
numbers: 17 LLMs on API-Bank and M3ToolEval. Up to 20% higher success and up to 30% fewer actions. CodeAct had higher success for 12 of 17 models. gpt-4-1106-preview: +20.7% absolute vs the next-best format (text) and 2.1 fewer turns on M3ToolEval. The paper says gains widen as model ability grows.
limits: Not a probe-vs-no-probe test; it compares the action format. 2024 models. Open-source models trail closed ones by a large margin.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to 'probing stops helping for strong models' (gap 4). Code is a good probe medium: composable and returns error text. Supports using code to probe counts, shapes and small cases.

source: Yoon et al. (2026) PaT: planning-after-trial for efficient test-time code generation (ACL 2026)
finding: Gaps 1, 3. Try first, plan only if the check fails, beat plan-first at lower cost on code tasks. A model solves about 76% of the standard problems directly, so planning on every problem is waste. This is a gate on an expensive step, here planning rather than probing.
numbers: Qwen3 4B/8B/14B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-Coder; HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+ average Pass@1 with cost normalised to one standard call. Qwen3-4B: Standard 76.05 (1.00); Best-of-N 76.95 (3.39); CodeT 76.63 (18.82); FunCoder (plan-first) 81.18 (8.31); PaT 83.13 (4.85). Qwen3-32B: Standard 83.35; FunCoder 87.66 (8.93); PaT 88.37 (5.09). A small generator plus a large planner matches a large model at about 69% less cost. On xCodeEval Qwen3-4B Pass@1 rose from 18.40 (standard) to 34.20 (PaT, cost 17.93).
limits: The gate is a failed verification, not a probe or a confidence estimate. Gains are on easy benchmarks; cost is relative to one call. Verification uses tests, so the signal quality depends on them.
agent_relevance: A gate that fires on a failed outside check is cheaper than always planning (or probing) and did not lose accuracy. Supports U2: gate by an outside signal, not always-on.

source: Shao et al. (2025) Do LLM agents know how to ground, recover, and assess? SeekBench
finding: Gap 3. Search agents often answer without enough evidence. Training with reinforcement learning reduced overconfident answering but lowered how well reasoning was tied to evidence.
numbers: 190 expert-annotated traces (over 1,800 steps) for annotation; 28,493 traces over seven QA benchmarks for evaluation. RL-trained agents: 31.6% accuracy when answering with good evidence vs 8.4% without supporting evidence. Overconfident answers: base 63.1%, few-shot 51.1%, RL-trained 35.3%; calibration error 0.329, 0.317, 0.309.
limits: Search/QA agents, not code probes. Calibration error differences are small. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Evidence that 'do I have enough information to answer?' is a decision agents get wrong in the overconfident direction. A check before answering is a measured gap, not a guess.

source: Wang, Qian, Li et al. (2026) Position: agents should invoke external tools only when epistemically necessary (ICML 2026)
finding: Gap 3. Position paper with no new measurements. It names epistemic necessity as the criterion: call a tool only if the task cannot be done reliably by reasoning over the current context. It links overthinking and overacting to wrongly sized epistemic effort, and argues that unneeded delegation can stall internal reasoning.
numbers: No experiments. Framework called Theory of Agent.
limits: No data. Do not count as evidence of effect. The rule is stated, not tested.
agent_relevance: Gives plain wording for the gate: probe only if internal reasoning cannot settle the unknown. Test it as U2.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Understanding reasoning in LLMs through strategic information allocation under uncertainty
finding: Gap 10 (side). Without any outside signal, a bare doubt cue ('Wait, is that correct?') recovered some failed reasoning runs. This is internal and limited, and contrasts with probes that return outside data.
numbers: On failed trajectories a minimal doubt cue recovers around 15% of incorrect rollouts; as few as 800 training samples instil or suppress the habit. Qwen3 models on AIME24/25, AMC23, MATH500.
limits: Math reasoning, no tools. Recovery counts failed runs fixed, not net accuracy, so it does not contradict Huang et al. (d08). Only the abstract, introduction and recovery-rate sections were read closely.
agent_relevance: A small free gain exists from a doubt cue, but the net effect must be checked for flips of correct answers (U7).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Thinking before running! Efficient code generation with thorough exploration and optimal refinement (ThinkCoder)
finding: Gap 1. Exploring several candidate solutions before running and refining beat other multi-round methods at small cost. It is selection and refinement, not probing a hidden fact.
numbers: Pass@1 +3.0% over MapCoder at 6.4% of its compute; 0.5% higher than AgentCoder after 2 rounds vs AgentCoder's 5 rounds; LLaMA2-7B reaches competitive results with 20% of compute after ReST.
limits: Compared with other multi-agent systems, not a matched-budget direct-solve baseline. Older benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Little guidance for probes; shows that fewer, better-aimed rounds can match many rounds.

source: Gap 5 and 8 search record: independent replication of the Maglio preview effect; named-term LLM studies
finding: Gap 5 stays partly open. d01 already confirmed the odd statistics are printed in the original paper (df 59 with N=30; t=33.85 and t=2.01), so the flag in the critique is about the original, not a copying error. Web search this pass found no independent-lab replication of the preview-priming effect and nothing with N above 30. One further paper from the same research line (self priming in epistemic action expertise, IBM page) turned up but was not opened. Gap 8 is partly closed: one named-term LLM paper with experiments (d19) and one with epistemic ASK actions (d26) were found, besides the position papers.
numbers: 0 independent replications found; 2 named-term LLM papers opened (d19, d26) in addition to the 2026 position paper (c01) and d30.
limits: Search tools: WebSearch (6 calls used), arXiv API, direct fetches. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited. Absence is not proven.
agent_relevance: Treat the human priming result as same-lab evidence. The direct test of the hypothesis on an LLM is still ours to run.

source: Gap 1 search record: equal-token comparison of probe-first and attempt-first
finding: Gap 1 stays open. A targeted search for a matched-budget ablation of 'write a test or run a small experiment first' against 'attempt directly' found none. Closest items: PaT (d28, try first, gate on failure), TTI (d23, interaction vs per-step thinking), BRT (d22, reproduction test as input), Ceka (d21, observational).
numbers: 0 direct matched-budget studies found; 4 adjacent studies opened.
limits: Two search calls; an ablation inside a larger paper may not show in titles.
agent_relevance: The central test (U1) has no published answer. Run it.
